concerns.text: The plan cites 'YouTube Trending' (jettisonthenet/timeseries_trending_youtube_videos_2019-04-15_to_2020-04-15) as a time series for testing statistical robustness to autocorrelation. This dataset contains discrete event counts (views) per video, which are inherently non-stationary, zero-inflated, and lack the continuous temporal dependence structure required to model ARFIMA/fGn processes or test t-test robustness in the manner described. The data represents a collection of independent items with timestamps, not a continuous time series of a single variable evolving over time. Using this dataset for the proposed ACF/Hurst analysis will yield spurious results or fail to meet the 'continuous time series' assumption of the statistical tests.

The plan cites 'UCI HAR' (udayl/UCI_HAR) as a source for 'shorter, high-frequency sensor data' to test robustness to non-independence. The UCI HAR dataset consists of accelerometer/gyroscope readings from human subjects performing specific activities. The data is segmented into fixed-length windows (2.56s) for activity classification, not a continuous long-range time series. The temporal dependence is short-range and bounded by the activity window, making it unsuitable for estimating long-range dependence metrics (Hurst exponent) or testing the robustness of t-tests to the specific type of non-independence (long-memory processes) the study aims to quantify.

The plan cites 'Energy Time Series' (nenils/time_series_energy) as a source for 'continuous power load data'. The dataset name and source (nenils/time_series_energy) appear to be a generic or potentially mislabeled repository. Without a verified, specific dataset ID or a clear description of the variable (e.g., 'UK Power Load' vs. 'Household Power Consumption'), it is unclear if this dataset provides the continuous, long-duration series required for Hurst exponent estimation. If the dataset is a collection of short household traces rather than a grid-level load series, it may not exhibit the long-range dependence necessary for the study's core hypothesis.
